User's words: "when the session list is presented. When the selected line is not a session but the 'exit' option, do not allow the 'n' key, nor display the option in the status bar. Same is true for the 'x' key."

What the code does now (src/menu.rs). rows() builds [sessions..., New (single-host menu only), Exit]. With the cursor on Exit:

- n (menu.rs:328) matches (false, _) in a single-host menu and returns Choice::New { host: 0 }, so it really does make a new session from the exit row. In the every-host menu the (true, _) arm only sets a note.
- x (menu.rs:313) is already a no-op off a session row (`if let Row::Session(..)`), but silently: nothing tells the user why.
- The key bar (menu.rs:447-450) is one fixed string, "1-9, or up/down jk and Enter: attach   .: <all|detached only>   x: end   n: new<there>   Esc: leave", drawn the same whatever the cursor is on.

Done when the bar lists only the keys that act on the row under the cursor (no "x: end" or "n: new" on Exit), n on the exit row does nothing instead of creating a session, and tests/menu.rs covers both: the bar's text on the exit row, and n on the exit row leaving the menu unchanged.

Open question for whoever takes it: the New row has the same shape (x does nothing there, and "Enter: attach" is wrong on both New and Exit). Worth deciding whether the rule is "hide keys that do not apply to this row" in general, or just the exit row the user named.

Follows acs-s0g, which built the menu.
close_reason: Implemented in #104: the key bar is built per row and n/x act only where they apply

title: List sessions on every host in the configuration
description:
Show the sessions on all configured hosts in one command.

User's ask: "add a way to display all the sessions on all hosts that are in the configuration".

Today `acs <host> --list` (src/list.rs) lists one host. The configuration's `hosts:` aliases (DESIGN §7.2, §7.3; src/config.rs, src/alias.rs) name every host acs knows.

Proposed shape (settle during implementation):

- `acs --list` with no host (or `acs list`, which would become a reserved first argument like `config` and `upgrade`) lists every alias.
- Each alias is resolved the way a connection would be (ping check, fallback hosts), then asked via the same `_proxy --list` side call. Hosts are queried in parallel with a timeout, so one slow or down host does not hold up the rest.
- Output: the existing table with a HOST (alias) column, or one block per alias. An unreachable host, or one without acs of our version, gets one line saying so rather than failing the whole command.
- Exit status: 0 if every host answered, non-zero (for example 255) if any did not.

Done when tests cover several aliases, including an unreachable one and one without acs installed, using the fake transport and ping; README and DESIGN document the command.
close_reason: Implemented with tests: acs --list without a host lists every alias (PR #21, feat: list sessions on every configured host)

title: Reject a non-https ACS_RELEASES_URL and ignore it under elevated privileges
description:
Security, update integrity. release.rs takes the release base from ACS_RELEASES_URL with no scheme validation, so http:// and file:// are accepted (scripts/test_install.sh uses file:// deliberately). It is read by `acs upgrade`, by the detached `acs _update-check`, and by scripts/install.sh. Because the sums come from that same base, integrity checking is bypassed entirely, and the download is then executed.

Attack: a local user who can influence the environment of a privileged run (sudo -E, a sudoers env_keep, a poisoned shell rc, a CI step) points it at their own server and gets code execution as the upgrading user. The docs themselves suggest `sudo acs upgrade`. It also downgrades a mirror to cleartext for a network attacker.

Done when a non-https base is refused unless an explicit opt-out flag is passed, the variable is ignored when the effective uid differs from the real uid, the test suite's file:// use goes through the opt-out, and a test covers each case.
close_reason: Implemented in #115: https required unless flagged, and ignored under a privilege mismatch

title: local_networks tests the wrong address: replace it with a caller-side per-host setting
description:
User's words: "the current implementation does not do what it's intended for.. File a bead to both remove current implementation and implement the correct one". On why a host entry cannot carry the setting: "The idea is that by specifying the local_networks on a host, the host will get preferred if the calling host is in any of the local_networks".

`local_networks` (acs-c9d, shipped in v0.11.0) tests the wrong address. It is a **target-side** filter when it needed to be a **caller-side** gate, and the difference is not cosmetic: as built, a configured network ranks a host first *wherever you are*.

## The defect

`prefer_local_network` on its own is correct and should stay. Its list comes from `getifaddrs`, so it is **self-gating**: the networks in it change as the machine moves, and "the host's address is on a network I am directly attached to" is a true statement about locality however you test it.

`local_networks` appends static entries to that same list (src/alias.rs:50):

```rust
n.local.extend(config.local_networks_for(alias).value.iter().copied());
```

and the match tests the **host's** resolved addresses against it (src/alias.rs:207, `addrs` from `resolve(&host, …)`):

```rust
on_net[i] = netmatch::matching(&network.local, &addrs);
```

So appending a static network destroys exactly the gating that made the interface-derived list meaningful. With `local_networks: [172.16.0.0/16]`, a host at 172.16.8.2 is ranked first from a coffee shop on 10.0.0.0/8 just as it is from the office, because the only address consulted is the host's. The caller's own address is never tested — the machine's interfaces merely *contribute entries to the list*.

The damage is bounded but real: the mis-ranked host still has to answer its ping, so you pay a `reachability_timeout` (500 ms default) and fall through to the right host. The ordering is simply wrong and the ping gate hides it.

## Why it got through review

acs-c9d's worked example — O at 172.16.1.65, T at 172.16.8.2, `local_networks: [172.16.0.0/16]` — gives the **same answer under both readings**: under the built rule T's address is in the /16, under the intended one O's address is. The one example in the bead, the README (README.md:345-353), DESIGN §7.3 and the tests could not tell the two apart. acs-c9d even flagged the ambiguity in as many words — "the user's phrasing, 'local for this host', reads as per alias (and maybe per host entry), while the example is about what O believes" — and then resolved it the other way.

## Remove

Not in production, so a clean break: no deprecated alias, no compatibility branch, no migration path. An existing config with a global or per-alias `local_networks:` should become a plain unknown-key error.

- src/config.rs: the `Config.local_networks` field (:129), `Alias.local_networks` (:99), `local_networks` from `KEYS` (:166) and `ALIAS_KEYS` (:199), the `NETWORKS` const (:211), `local_networks_for` (:510), the `networks_mut`/`networks_setting` arms (:420, :427) and the alias merge (:753).
- src/config.rs parsing: `networks_value` (:627), `parse_networks` (:649), `format_networks` (:659) — or keep them, since the new setting parses the same CIDR list; decide rather than delete blindly.
- src/config_cmd.rs: the `NETWORKS` branch in `typed` (:93), `networks_node` (:76), the `Seq` join in `value_text` (:108), and the alias-settings help text (:42, :47).
- src/alias.rs:50 — the `extend` that is the defect itself.
- Tests: the acs-c9d round-trip test `local_networks_read_as_a_list_globally_and_per_alias` (src/config.rs:1419), `a_configured_network_counts_as_local_in_either_family` (src/alias.rs:833), `networks_alone_do_nothing_without_prefer_local_network` (src/alias.rs:894), and the CLI test in tests/config_cmd.rs:162. Note that the single-scalar cases added in #137 go with them — that PR tested the parsing, which may survive, not the semantics, which do not.
- Docs: README.md:319-320 and :345-353, docs/DESIGN.md:906, :935, :1011-1032, :1180, :1184.

## Implement

`local_networks` becomes a **host-entry** setting (`HOST_KEYS`, src/config.rs:180, today `host, user, reachability_check, identity_file, persist, prefer`): a list of CIDR networks, IPv4 and IPv6, meaning *prefer this entry when the calling machine is on one of these*.

The test inverts. Instead of `matching(nets, host_addrs)`, it is the client's own `getifaddrs` addresses against the entry's list. `netmatch::LocalNet::contains` already masks both sides and handles both families (netmatch.rs:28-40), so the arithmetic is there; what changes is which value is passed as the address and which as the network. A caller-side hit needs no name resolution at all, which also makes it cheaper than the current path.

Ranking (`alias::rank`, src/alias.rs:215-224) keeps its shape — local first, then `prefer`, then configured order — with "local" now meaning *either* the interface-derived match *or* a caller-side `local_networks` hit.

## Scope decisions to make when taking this

- **Does the new setting require `prefer_local_network: true`?** Today `local_networks` is inert without it (`.then(network)` short-circuits, src/alias.rs:48). An explicit per-host statement arguably should stand on its own; the counter-argument is one switch governing all locality preference. Decide and document.
- **Is there still a global or per-alias form?** Probably not: "prefer *which* host when I am in network X" does not parse without naming the host, which is why per-entry is the right home. Say so explicitly rather than leaving the absence unexplained.
- **Several entries match.** Configured order, or the longest prefix? `rank` is a stable sort, so configured order is the no-work answer.
- **`-v` wording.** The existing line is "<alias>: <host> is on the local network <net>" (src/alias.rs:133), which describes the old direction. The caller-side one reads more like "this machine is on <net>, so <host> is preferred".

## Done when

A host entry accepts `local_networks`, that entry is ranked first exactly when one of **this machine's own** addresses falls in one of its networks, a global or per-alias `local_networks` is an unknown-key error, `prefer_local_network`'s interface-derived behaviour is unchanged, a bad CIDR is still a clear config error, and tests cover IPv4 and IPv6 plus the case the old design got wrong — **a host inside the configured network that is NOT preferred because the caller is somewhere else**, which is the regression test for this bead. README and DESIGN §7.3 describe the caller-side direction in a sentence that could not also describe the target-side one.

Supersedes acs-c9d; extends acs-sia.
close_reason: Fixed in #148: local_networks is now a caller-side per-host setting

title: Compare pre-release identifiers numerically in release::compare
description:
release::compare (src/release.rs:84-93) uses (Some(x), Some(y)) => x.cmp(y), so 0.3.0-rc10 < 0.3.0-rc2 ("rc10".cmp("rc2") is Less). Semver compares dot-separated numeric identifiers numerically. Impact is limited because find_asset refuses any archive whose version has a "-", so releases are never pre-releases; only decide()/should_link() for locally built -dev/-rc versions are affected. Related: archive_target("armv7-unknown-linux-musleabihf") (release.rs:27-32) yields the non-existent armv7-unknown-linux-musl; harmless while no armv7 archive is published.

Done when identifiers are split on "." and numeric ones compared as numbers, with a unit test for rc2 < rc10.
close_reason: Implemented in #89 (a3f0478)

title: Scrub the inherited ssh and agent environment from the session shell
description:
Security, credential reuse inside a shared account. master.rs start_child removes only ACS_SOCKET_DIR and ACS_MASTER_LOG, so the session shell inherits the creating ssh login's SSH_AUTH_SOCK, SSH_CONNECTION, SSH_CLIENT, KRB5CCNAME, DISPLAY, XDG_SESSION_ID and DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS, keeps them for the life of the session, and never refreshes them for later attachers.

So alice creates a session with agent forwarding, bob attaches on the same account, and bob's shell uses alice's forwarded agent for onward ssh as long as alice's connection lives. Everyone else's shell meanwhile reports alice's laptop in SSH_CONNECTION and DISPLAY. No privilege boundary is crossed, since the same uid could read /proc anyway, but acs hands it over invisibly and permanently.

Done when the forwarding and session variables are scrubbed from the child environment, or re-exported per attach from the attaching connection, whichever DESIGN §4.5 prefers, with the choice documented and a test.
close_reason: Implemented in #130: the session shell inherits no ssh or agent environment

title: Let prefer_local_network take explicit networks counted as local
description:
User's words: "as an extension to 'prefer_local_network' add the ability to specify one or more networks, ipv4 or ipv6 that are considered local for this host. As an example, the target T is at 172.16.8.2 and the origin O is on 172.16.1.65, it would not select T. However after specifying that 172.16.0.0/16 is local to T, O would match and use this host."

Today (acs-sia, DESIGN §7.3) the only networks that count are the ones this machine's own interfaces are on: netmatch::local_networks() reads getifaddrs and builds a LocalNet { addr, prefix } per address, alias::resolve filters to `!n.local.is_empty()`, and netmatch::matching() ranks a host first when one of its resolved A/AAAA addresses falls in one of those. So O on 172.16.1.65/24 never matches T at 172.16.8.2: the interface prefix is too narrow, although both are on the same site.

Wanted: a configured list of CIDR networks, IPv4 and IPv6, added to the machine's own for that match. With 172.16.0.0/16 configured, O ranks T as local and uses it.

Notes for whoever takes it:

- netmatch::LocalNet and contains() already do the arithmetic for both families, and usable() rejects a zero prefix, so the matching side needs little more than parsing "addr/prefix" into a LocalNet.
- The config side is the new part: every setting today is a scalar (bool or duration; see config.rs ALIAS_BOOLS and the tables config_cmd.rs uses for `acs config set`), so this is the first list-valued one. It needs a type in Setting, a parser with a real error for a bad CIDR, printing in `acs config show`, and a decision on `acs config set` syntax for a list.
- Decide the scope and say so in the doc: the user's phrasing, "local for this host", reads as per alias (and maybe per host entry), while the example is about what O believes. Global plus per-alias matches how prefer_local_network already resolves (config.rs:464), and per-entry is the third option.

Done when the networks can be configured, they are merged with the interface-derived ones for the ranking, a bad CIDR is a clear config error, netmatch and alias tests cover an IPv4 and an IPv6 case that only match through a configured network, and README plus DESIGN §7.3 document it.

Extends acs-sia.
close_reason: Implemented in #106 (v0.11.0): the local_networks setting, global and per alias

title: Quote the version in ssh::prelude and remote_candidates
description:
Security, latent command injection. ssh.rs remote_candidates interpolates the version into "$HOME/.local/share/acs/{version}/acs" with no quoting, and prelude puts that inside double quotes, where $, backtick and backslash are still live. Its sibling args all go through sh_quote, and install.rs does sh_quote the version, so this is an inconsistency rather than a deliberate exception. Verified by reading both.

Not exploitable today: every caller passes the compile-time crate::VERSION. But both functions are pub, take &str, and document no constraint, so one future caller passing a configured or remote-supplied version makes it remote code execution through both shell layers.

Done when the version is quoted the same way the other arguments are (or the function takes a validated type), with a test using a hostile version string.
close_reason: Implemented in #125: the version is quoted, and the prelude no longer re-wraps it

title: Ignore frames from a taken-over or detached (Closing) connection
description:
`handle()` (src/master.rs ~L553-591) has no check for `ConnState::Closing`. A Closing conn is not polled for POLLIN, but POLLHUP is always reported, so when the old client's proxy closes, `read_conn` decodes whatever was still buffered and applies it as for the active client: INPUT goes to the pty and advances `InputDedupe::written`, so the new client's first keystrokes at the same sequence are dropped as duplicates (DESIGN §5.1 says clients taking turns never collide); RESIZE resizes the new client's pty; KILL kills the session. Trigger: the old client types or resizes between the takeover and its exit on TAKEOVER, or its proxy holds unsent input when the link died.

Done when Closing conns are drained without handling (or skipped in read_conn), with a test that a late INPUT/RESIZE/KILL from a taken-over conn is ignored and the new client's input_seq stays consistent.
close_reason: Fixed with regression tests (bugs-master branch)

title: Drain queued output to the client before failing on a master write error
description:
In `relay()` (src/proxy.rs ~L266) `flush(m, &mut to_master)?` propagates EPIPE when the master closed between this iteration's `read(m)` — which just queued the EXIT frame into `to_client` — and the write. `session()` then errors out without `drain(STDOUT, &to_client)`, so the client sees "link lost" and later NO_SESSION instead of the child's exit status. Needs queued client input (a PING or INPUT) in the same iteration, so the window is narrow.

Done when a write error to the master falls through to the drain path instead of `?`, with a test for EOF-with-pending-output ordering.
close_reason: Fixed with regression tests (bugs-master branch)

title: Do not ACK input the master has not written to the pty
description:
The master ACKs INPUT when it enters pty_in (src/master.rs:622-630), not when it is written; write_pty (master.rs:860-878) clears pty_in on any error or when !pty_open, so acked input can be silently lost. The client then never resends it on resume because it believes the master has it. Only observable on a pty write error, so rare, but it breaks the §5.2 guarantee that an ACK means written.

Done when the ACK is sent after the write succeeds (or the sequence is only advanced by written bytes), with a test that fails the pty write and asserts no ACK.
close_reason: Implemented in #99 (d6cfc12)

title: Keep command mode working after Alt+_ and other ESC-prefixed keys
description:
In Lex::Esc (src/keys.rs:226-230) any of ] P _ ^ X after ESC switches the input lexer into Lex::Str, which (keys.rs:283-290) forwards every byte raw until a BEL or ESC \, and Lex::Str has no timeout (deadline()/tick() only cover seq_since and held state). It exists for terminal replies (OSC 52/11, DCS), but a keyboard Meta+key produces the same two bytes.

Scenario: in bash press Alt+_ (readline's default yank-last-arg, sent as ESC _). From then on Ctrl-] Ctrl-] d, legacy or kitty encoding, is forwarded to the program and never detaches, silently, until the user types Ctrl-G. Verified in a scratch harness: ESC _ then 5 s later 1D 1D 64 gives action=None with all bytes forwarded; with a 07 in between it detaches. Contradicts the README's "press Ctrl-] Ctrl-] quickly, then d".

Done when only the string introducers the replies actually use are treated as strings and the string state is bounded by a short timeout like PENDING_MS, with a test for ESC _ followed by the command key.
close_reason: Implemented in #73 (0f6159f)

title: Require a handshake and authorize KILL on the master
description:
Security, missing authorization. master.rs handles `Msg::Kill if pending` by setting the connection to Ending and calling start_kill() with no HELLO, no identity and no force flag. Verified by reading the arm. The BUSY path leaves the connection Pending, so a client that was just refused ("busy, alice@laptop is attached") can send a 5-byte KILL frame on that same connection and destroy the session it was denied. More simply, any process running as that uid can write the frame into any session socket. The menu's confirmation is client-side courtesy only.

The socket permission is therefore the entire trust boundary, which DESIGN §4.5 accepts for a shared account while still promising nobody ends someone else's session by accident.

Done when KILL requires a completed HELLO and is subject to the same identity and force rules as a takeover, a KILL on a connection already answered BUSY is refused, the proxy's END_SESSION path still works, and tests cover the refused-then-kill sequence.
close_reason: Implemented in #111: KILL carries its asker and is held to the takeover rule

title: Check GitHub weekly for a newer acs release and show a message
description:
Check GitHub for a newer acs release once a week and tell the user.

User's ask: "have the acs binary check for a new release on github once a week, if a new release is available display a message".

Proposed design:

- Only the local client checks; the remote roles (`_proxy`, `_master`, `_install`) never do.
- At most once every 7 days, recorded in `$XDG_STATE_HOME/acs/update-check` (default `~/.local/state/acs/update-check`). It queries `https://api.github.com/repos/michel-onstein/acs/releases/latest` and compares `tag_name` to our version with semver.
- acs has no HTTP/TLS client, and adding one would break the 1 MB size budget (DESIGN §9). So it shells out to `curl` with a short timeout (for example `-m 3`) and never blocks or delays connecting: run it in the background and show the result on the next start, or finish within the timeout before raw mode.
- The message goes to stderr outside the session stream, e.g. `acs 0.3.0 is available (you have 0.2.0) — run: acs upgrade`. It is shown once per new version, not on every run.
- Can be turned off with `ACS_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1`, and with an `update_check: false` option once the YAML config file (acs-xfk) exists. Being offline or rate-limited stays silent.

Done when: unit tests cover the interval, the version comparison and the "shown once" state; an integration test injects the API response (e.g. a fake curl on PATH); README documents it and how to turn it off.
close_reason: Implemented: weekly background _update-check (SHA256SUMS via curl, 3 s), state in XDG_STATE_HOME, message once per new version before connecting, off via ACS_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1 or update_check: false; silent offline

title: Explain the README's two alias shapes: a host list, or a mapping
description:
Wanted: the README's example configuration uses two shapes for an alias without saying why. `devbox` and `nas` are a list of host entries, while `lab` is a mapping of its own settings with the entries under `hosts:`. A reader asked whether the example is even correct.

Verified (v0.8.1): the example is valid. Loaded as-is with the installed acs, `acs config host list` resolves all five hosts with the expected user, check and key. Both shapes are by design (DESIGN §7.2, "An alias's own settings"): YAML cannot make one node both a list and a mapping, so an alias with a setting of its own (`identity_file`, `redraw_on_reconnect`, `reachability_timeout`, `persist`, `reachability_interval`) must be a mapping, and its hosts then need a key. The list form stays the short, usual one. `acs config host set` / `unset` convert between the two. The README's only hint is the comment "an alias with settings of its own", plus the settings-table row for `hosts`.

Change: one or two sentences in README "Configuration" next to the example (or under "Host aliases"): an alias is a list of hosts, or, when it has settings of its own, a mapping of those settings plus `hosts:` with the list. The mapping form is always allowed, and `acs config host set` rewrites a list-form alias into it. Word it to match the top-level key's name at the time; a rename of that key is being proposed separately.

Done when the README explains both shapes and when each is needed, markdownlint passes (scripts/verify.sh), and nothing else changes.
close_reason: Done in PR #60 (8a9e909): the README explains the list and mapping alias shapes

title: Validate the version parsed out of SHA256SUMS in the installer script
description:
Security, path traversal in the shell installer. scripts/install.sh greps SHA256SUMS with a pattern whose filename part is [^ ]+, which permits / and .., so the extracted version can be something like 1.0/../../../../etc/cron.d/x. That value then reaches mkdir -p "$lib/$version" and the place call, as root in the root branch. The Rust side is strict about this (release::find_asset then parse_version, digits and dots only), so the two implementations of the same logic disagree.

Reaching it needs full control of the release channel, so this is hardening behind the signing item rather than an independent hole, and the fetch into $tmp/$file fails first for most traversal shapes.

Done when the script requires X.Y.Z exactly, as the Rust code does, and tests/scripts.rs or test_install.sh covers a hostile sums line.
close_reason: Implemented in #126: the sums pattern requires X.Y.Z, with a case guard behind it

title: Fix master spinning on pty POLLHUP while the ring is full
description:
With an active client stalled and the ring full (`room_before_overwrite(next) == 0`) the master polls the pty with `events = 0` (src/master.rs ~L384-395), but Linux `n_tty_poll` reports POLLHUP once the slave side closes, regardless of `events` and even with unread data. Poll then returns immediately, `read_pty` bails at `want == 0` (~L793-796), the drained heuristic does not apply because `asked` is false, `pump_output` cannot add (client at high water), and the loop spins hot until the client drains a chunk or the connection dies. Trigger: `acs host -- cat big.log` over a stalled link when cat finishes.

Done when the pty fd is omitted from the poll set (or the loop sleeps) while `room == 0`, with a test covering hangup-while-stalled.
close_reason: Fixed with regression tests (bugs-master branch)

title: Harden the session socket: fchmod 0600 and an O_NOFOLLOW directory handle
description:
Security, defence in depth. Two small gaps sit under an otherwise solid cross-uid boundary. master.rs bind creates the unix socket at 0777 masked by the inherited umask and never chmods it; the 0700 directory and the SO_PEERCRED/getpeereid check on every accept are the only controls. session.rs checks the directory with symlink_metadata and then calls set_permissions by PATH, a chmod that follows symlinks applied after the lstat, and only the leaf's ownership is checked, never its ancestors.

Neither is exploitable at the default path: /tmp is sticky, a pre-created directory fails the uid check, and tests/multiuser.rs deliberately loosens the directory to 0755 and the socket to 0777 and proves the peer check still refuses. It becomes reachable only with ACS_SOCKET_DIR pointed at a path whose parent others can write, where swapping the leaf for a symlink between the check and the connect redirects the client to an attacker's master.

Done when the socket is fchmod'd 0600 after bind, the directory is verified and chmod'd through an O_DIRECTORY|O_NOFOLLOW handle rather than by path, a socket directory with other-writable ancestors is refused, and multiuser tests cover it.
close_reason: Implemented in #131: socket created 0600, dir held by an O_NOFOLLOW handle, ancestors checked

title: Guard the input-dedupe sequence arithmetic against overflow
description:
Security, peer-steerable arithmetic. resume.rs InputDedupe::accept computes `let end = seq + bytes.len() as u64;` with no guard, where seq comes straight from a peer's INPUT frame, and master.rs written_to_pty then does a plain `self.input.written() - self.pty_in.len() as u64`. Verified by reading both, and Cargo.toml sets no overflow-checks, so release builds wrap.

An INPUT frame with seq near u64::MAX wraps end to a small number while bytes are queued, so written_to_pty underflows to roughly 2^64 and poisons the ACK the client uses to decide what it may forget. A debug build aborts the master outright, ending the session.

Done when the addition is checked and a frame whose sequence cannot be valid is refused as a protocol error rather than wrapping, with a test for the wrapping sequence.
close_reason: Implemented in #127: accept refuses a sequence whose end does not fit

title: Add acs config subcommands to edit the configuration
description:
Add `acs config …` subcommands to manage the configuration file from the command line.

User's ask: "add options to the cli to allow configuration of acs through the command line, something like `acs config host add <alias> <hostname> --reachability-check`".

Proposed shape (settle the details during implementation):

- `acs config show`: prints the merged configuration and which file each value came from.
- `acs config get <key>` and `acs config set <key> <value>`, e.g. `acs config set install_on_remote false`.
- `acs config host add <alias> <host> [--user U] [--no-reachability-check]`: appends an entry, so repeated adds give an alias fallback hosts in order.
- `acs config host remove <alias> [<host>]` and `acs config host list`.
- Writes go to the local file (`~/.config/acs/config.yaml`); `--global` targets `/etc/acs/config.yaml` and needs the right permissions.

Notes:

- `config` becomes a reserved first argument. Today it would be read as a host name (src/cli.rs), so a host literally called `config` needs a way through, e.g. `acs -- config` or `user@config`. Document it.
- Writing must keep the file readable and stable (no reordering of what it did not touch); comments are nice to keep but not required.

Done when: every subcommand works against a temp HOME in tests; errors (unknown key, wrong type, missing alias) are clear; README documents it.
close_reason: Implemented: acs config show/get/set/unset/path and host list/add/remove, --global, comment-preserving validated atomic writes; config reserved as first arg

title: Treat a failure to link ~/.local/bin/acs as a warning, not an install failure
description:
install::finish() (src/install.rs:266-278, 302-314) renames the binary into place and only then calls link_bin; any error there (HOME unset in the ssh environment, ~/.local/bin existing as a regular file or not writable, symlink failing) returns Err, the finisher exits 1 without printing ok, and the client reports "installing acs failed" and exits, although ~/.local/share/acs/<v>/acs is complete and every later connection works. DESIGN §8 says nothing in the protocol depends on that link.

Done when link_bin failure is reported as a warning after ok, the install still counts as successful, and a test makes ~/.local/bin a file and asserts the install succeeds with a warning.
close_reason: Implemented in #83 (80cf8d5)

title: Install creates its directory under the umask, then refuses to run from it
description:
Reported by the user against v0.11.4, connecting to a host that worked before:

    acs: installing acs 0.11.4 on tolot (Linux x86_64)…
    acs: installed acs 0.11.4 on tolot
    acs: refusing to run /home/michel/.local/share/acs/0.11.4/acs: it or its
      directory is writable by others, or not yours
    acs: acs was installed on tolot but the remote still cannot run it
      (is $HOME the same for ssh commands?)
    exit 254

acs-08m (#132) added the prelude's acs_safe check, which refuses a candidate
whose file OR its directory is group/other writable, or not owned by the
caller (ssh.rs prelude()). It did not change the install, which still creates
the directory with a bare `mkdir -p` under the remote's umask
(install.rs:129,138 — `set -e; mkdir -p {dir}; …`).

The binary is fine: the upload chmod 755's it, and write_exe sets 0755 for
real past the umask (acs-28b). Only the directories are left to the umask.

On the reported host (umask 002, uid 1000, per-user group):

    drwxr-xr-x  /home/michel                       fine, predates acs
    drwxr-xr-x  /home/michel/.local                fine
    drwxr-xr-x  /home/michel/.local/share          fine
    drwxrwxr-x  /home/michel/.local/share/acs      made by acs, group write
    drwxrwxr-x  /home/michel/.local/share/acs/0.11.4   made by acs  <- checked
    -rwxr-xr-x  /home/michel/.local/share/acs/0.11.4/acs   fine

acs_safe checks `dirname "$b"`, the version directory, so it refuses the
directory acs itself has just created. Every host with umask 002 is bricked
by an install: it succeeds and the very next exec is refused, 254. The
ownership half of the check passes (uid 1000 owns all of it); only the group
write bit trips it. Here the group is the user's own per-user group, so it is
harmless in fact — but the check cannot know that, and should not have to.

Wanted: the install creates the directories it owns with 0755 explicitly,
past the umask, as it already does for the binary — the version directory
and its ~/.local/share/acs parent. Do not touch $HOME, ~/.local or
~/.local/share: acs did not create them, and chmod'ing a user's own
directories is not acs's business (the check does not look at them either).

Note for whoever takes it: an existing install on such a host stays broken
until its directory is fixed, since the directory is only created when a
version is new. Upgrading to the fixed version creates a new version
directory, so it heals itself; the stale ~/.local/share/acs parent should be
chmod'd by the install too so it does not linger group-writable.

Done when the install sets the mode on the directories it creates, a test
runs the real install script under umask 002 and asserts the resulting
directory is not group- or other-writable and that the real prelude then
execs it, and DESIGN §8 says the directories are created 0755 past the umask.

Regression of acs-08m; the mode-past-umask reasoning is acs-28b's.
close_reason: Fixed in #138 (v0.11.5): the install sets 0755 on the directories it makes

title: Make the timing-sensitive tests survive a loaded machine
description:
Two integration tests fail intermittently when the whole suite runs at once, and pass on their own every time. Seen twice during the security burn-down of 2026-09-20:

- tests/master.rs::a_client_that_vanishes_without_closing_is_dropped — pushes 3 MB through a pty and waits on a marker file within a 10 s deadline.
- tests/reconnect.rs::ctrl_c_during_a_redial_clears_the_status_line — depends on a redial landing inside a window.

Neither was a real failure: re-running scripts/verify.sh passed both times, and the changes in flight (an installer digest check, an input-sequence guard) cannot touch either path. But a gate that fails one run in several teaches people to re-run rather than to read, which is how a real failure eventually gets waved through.

Done when both are steady under `cargo test` with the whole suite running in parallel — a generous deadline driven by an environment knob as the liveness tests already use, waiting on a condition rather than a sleep, or serialising the few that need the machine to themselves — and the reason is written next to whichever mechanism is chosen.
close_reason: Implemented in #135: generous deadlines, a condition instead of a sleep, a wider parallel margin

title: Draw the session menu's selection bar at one width for every row
description:
Wanted, in the user's words: "in the session selection menu, make the bar that shows your current selection the same width across all the entries, covering the largest width needed among the entries."

Verified (v0.5.0, src/menu.rs `Menu::render`): each selectable row is `"{mark} {key}  {text}"` and the cursor's row is written as `\x1b[7m{text}\x1b[0m`, so the reversed bar is exactly as long as that row's text. It is short on "new session" and "exit", and differs between sessions whose last `--list` column (the command) differs in length. It jumps in width as the cursor moves.

Fix: pad the cursor's row with spaces to the widest selectable row (sessions, new session, exit) currently shown, clipped at the terminal width (`cols`) as lines already are, so the bar never wraps. Measure in terminal columns rather than chars if a command can hold wide characters; `render` truncates with `chars().take(cols)` today.

Done when the reversed bar has the same width on every row, equal to the widest entry (or the terminal width if that is narrower), with a unit test next to the existing render tests in src/menu.rs asserting the padded width on a short row (exit) and a long session row.
close_reason: Implemented in PR #42 (01c9b5c): the selection bar is padded to the widest row, clipped at the terminal width, measured in columns

title: Let a fork set its release signing key at build time, as it now can the releases URL
description:
Follow-up to acs-5em (PR #153, be220ed), which made the default releases URL
settable at build time via `ACS_DEFAULT_RELEASES_URL`. The signing key did not
move with it, and the two are only useful together.

`signature::key_for(base)` returns the built-in `RELEASE_KEY` when `base ==
DEFAULT_RELEASES_URL`, and only otherwise consults `ACS_RELEASE_KEY`. So a fork
that bakes in its own releases URL and keeps acs's key **cannot verify its own
releases**: `acs upgrade` reaches the fork's SHA256SUMS and then refuses them,
because the key it checks against is upstream's. The fork's two options today
are to patch `src/signature.rs` (a merge conflict on every upstream sync — the
exact problem acs-5em removed for the URL) or to tell every user to export
`ACS_RELEASE_KEY` forever.

The mechanism to copy already exists and is one commit old: `build.rs` passes
the variable through with `cargo:rerun-if-env-changed`, `src/release.rs` has
`const fn default_releases_url(Option<&'static str>)` with an empty value
counting as unset, and `release::tests::the_default_releases_url_can_be_set_at_build_time`
is the shape of the test.

Note this is *not* a loosening of acs-95w or of acs-o9v's verification. The
runtime `ACS_RELEASE_KEY` override and its guards stay exactly as they are; a
compile-time key is chosen by whoever builds the binary, who already decides
what it does. Say so in the doc comment, as acs-5em did for the URL.

Done when the default release key can be set at build time and falls back to
today's `RELEASE_KEY` when unset, an empty value counts as unset, a test covers
both cases the way the URL's does, and the Forking table in docs/VERSIONING.md
moves the key from "source edit" to "build-time knob".

title: Take the create lock before --list removes a stale socket
description:
`list()` (src/proxy.rs ~L317-325) removes a socket after ECONNREFUSED/ENOENT without holding `create_lock`, while master start (src/master.rs ~L304-315) does check → unlink → bind under that lock. Interleaving: list connects (refused, old stale file) → master A unlinks the stale file and binds a fresh socket → list unlinks A's *live* socket. A is unreachable for up to `rebind_every()` (60 s); any proxy in that window spawns master B; when A's `check_socket` runs it sees another inode and leaves it — A is orphaned forever with its shell still running.

Done when the refused → unlink step takes `dir.create_lock(name)` (try_lock; skip if busy), with a test for list racing a bind.
close_reason: Fixed with regression tests (bugs-master branch)

title: Replace acs --list without a host by an acs list subcommand
description:
Wanted, in the user's words: "`acs --list` lists the sessions on all hosts. This is wrong: --list is an option style, not a command. It should be `acs list`. This does increase the number of reserved aliases/hosts."

Verified (v0.7.0): `acs [ssh options] --list` (or `-l`) with no host lists every alias's sessions (src/cli.rs, "Only `--list` goes without a host"; src/list.rs `run_all`; DESIGN §7.3 "Every alias at once"; README "Use"; `acs --help`). The other whole-program actions are already subcommands: `config` and `upgrade` are reserved **first** arguments (DESIGN §7.4, §7.5), and a host literally named like one is reached as `user@config` or with an option before it (`acs -p 22 config`). `list` becomes the third reserved first argument, with the same escape.

Change: `acs list` (taking the ssh options, as `acs --list` does today, e.g. `acs -p 2222 list` or `acs list -v`, whichever the parser settles on) runs today's all-alias listing (parallel, BatchMode, the HOST table). Drop the hostless `--list` outright, with no alias kept (not yet a compatibility contract; say so in the PR). Open point: whether the per-host `acs <host> --list` stays as an option (it is a modifier of a host) or moves to `acs list <host>` for symmetry. Decide and write it down in DESIGN.

Done when `acs list` lists every alias, a hostless `acs --list` is a usage error that points to `acs list`, `list` is documented as reserved with the `user@list` / option-before escape, cli.rs tests cover the parse (including a host named `list`), and DESIGN §4.4/§7.3/§7.4, the README, the module docs in cli.rs and `acs --help` are updated.
close_reason: Implemented in PR #45 (f5164ab): acs list [host] replaces the -l/--list option; list is a reserved first argument

title: Automatic semantic versioning (scripts/version-bump.sh)
description: Bump the version automatically after each merge: PATCH for small fixes, MINOR for larger fixes and features, MAJOR only on explicit instruction (resets MINOR and PATCH). Reads unreleased commits since the last vX.Y.Z tag, updates Cargo.toml/Cargo.lock, pushes a chore(release) commit and tag to origin/main via a throwaway worktree. Run by the ship skill.

title: Publish release binaries to GitHub Releases
description: Attach per-platform archives (acs-<version>-<target>.tar.gz), SHA256SUMS and install notes to a GitHub Release for each vX.Y.Z tag, built from the exact tag. scripts/release-binaries.sh does it; scripts/version-bump.sh calls it after cutting a release so shipping publishes binaries. Packaging lives in cargo xtask package (tested).
